Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.

- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

First Nations leaders in Alberta say ballot shortages, late-opening polling stations and identification rules obstructed some Indigenous voters during Monday’s provincial referendum. The nonbinding vote asked whether Alberta should begin legal steps toward a future separation referendum; about three-quarters of voters chose to remain in Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith said she would not call another separation vote while she is premier [aptnnews.ca#1][cbc.ca#5][thestar.com#1]. Treaty 8 campaign manager Jay Telegdi said he received reports of voters turned away because of identification and polling problems. Elections Alberta said it delivered extra ballots to five First Nations communities, three of which received multiple deliveries. The agency said 36 First Nations communities participated, up from 33 in 2023 [cbc.ca#5][theglobeandmail.com#11]. Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot called for changes to prevent similar barriers in future elections [aptnnews.ca#3]. The count on the nine other ballot questions remained unsettled Tuesday. Preliminary results showed support for all five immigration proposals and close contests on constitutional measures; Smith said she would pursue immigration reforms in the months and years ahead. items.title: [Fast Company] FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.

items.title: [Fast Company] AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] Meshtastic Offline GPS Tracking: Save Your Route Without a Phone
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A Meshtastic device can send its GPS position over the air, but that is not the same as keeping a track on the device itself. In the standard setup I was using, disconnecting the phone meant the node continued broadcasting its location without saving a local history for later. I wanted something simple: take a node out for a walk, leave the phone disconnected, and download the route when I got home. So I modified the Meshtastic firmware to add on-device GPS location caching. I have this running on a SenseCAP T1000E and a Heltec T096. Both remain Meshtastic nodes, with their normal communication functions, but now they can also record a route independently of the phone. Key Takeaways The custom firmware records GPS points on the node without a connected phone. A 500-point cache provides roughly eight hours of recording at one point per minute. Reconnect to Meshtastic to load saved positions, then export them as GPX. Clearing app history does not clear the tracker cache; use the device controls to remove saved points. Table of ContentsWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware AddsUsing the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000ESyncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic AppExporting Your Route as a GPX FileClearing the Tracker CacheInstalling the Firmware and Exploring the CodeWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware Adds Meshtastic is open source, and its module system gives you a useful way to add your own functionality without creating an entirely separate application. My modification adds a local cache for GPS points, controls for starting and stopping recording, and a way to replay those saved positions into the Meshtastic app. The basic workflow is: Start tracking on the device. Go walking or travelling without a connected phone. Reconnect to the Meshtastic app afterward. Let the saved positions populate the map. Export the track to GPX if you want to use it elsewhere. The device still sends position updates over the air as normal. Local recording is an additional function, not a replacement for Meshtastic communication. You can still receive messages and hear the usual notification sounds while recording your route. 500 points, recorded once per minute In this build, I set the cache capacity to 500 location points. With automatic recording every minute, that gives you roughly eight hours of tracking capacity, provided the device has a GPS location to save. That figure describes the number of points the cache can hold, not a battery-life measurement. You can also build up a collection of points across separate outings. One of my test devices had 205 points collected during experiments over about a month, while the other contained routes from several days of walking. Using the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096 The T096 still has the familiar Meshtastic screens. I added one extra page for the tracker, showing whether recording is on or off and how many points are cached. For example, the display can show tracking switched off with 205 of 500 points cached. Stopping recording does not remove those points. They remain available to download later. To start recording: Navigate to the tracker screen. Long-press the button to open its menu. Select Start Tracking. Check that the tracker screen changes to Tracking On. With tracking enabled, the firmware saves a location every minute when a GPS position is available. The cached-point counter increases as points are recorded. A count of 205, for instance, becomes 206 after the next successful recording. To stop, open the menu again and select Stop Tracking. This stops the extra local recording function. The node continues doing its normal Meshtastic work, including sending positions according to its configuration. The same menu also includes Clear Cache, but save that until you have downloaded or exported anything you want to keep. Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000E The T1000E does not have a screen, so I implemented the tracker controls through its button. The idea is to make it useful on its own, without needing to pull out a phone just to start a walk. Button action Tracker function One press Save the current location to the cache. Two presses Start or stop automatic recording every minute. Three presses Clear the cached locations. A double press starts recording with an audible beep. While recording, the device beeps every minute as it records. Double-press again to stop. The single-press action is handy when you just want to record where you are right now, rather than run continuous tracking. It writes that current location into the same cache. These shortcuts belong to this custom firmware. They are not instructions for the standard T1000E firmware. Syncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic App Once you return, connect to the device through the Meshtastic app as usual. There is no separate tracker app required for this part. Scan for nearby devices in the app's connection screen. Select the node you used for recording. Open that node's details and its Position history. Allow the connection to finish and the cached positions to arrive. The position history may initially look empty. In my demonstration, the connection indicator was orange while connecting, then turned green. Once connected, the saved positions started arriving and the route filled in on the map. The saved points populate the map after the node reconnects. On my T096, the downloaded history included driving routes as well as the walking route I use regularly. Connecting to the T1000E brought in its own saved points from several days of walking. Apparently, I do quite a lot of walking! Deleting app history does not clear the device This is an important distinction: the app's position history and the device's cache are separate. I deleted the position history in the app, disconnected, and connected again. The device replayed the saved positions, and the route appeared again. The points were still on the node. So, if a route returns after you delete it from the phone, that is expected. To remove the source of that replay, you need to clear the cache on the tracker itself. Exporting Your Route as a GPX File Once the positions are in the Meshtastic app, you can export them as a GPX file and open the result in another mapping application. I exported a test track, gave it a name, then opened it through the file browser in GPX Viewer. The same route appeared there, this time drawn over its map. The process is straightforward: Wait for the cached positions to finish loading into Meshtastic. Use the position-history export option to save a GPX file. Give the file a name. Open it in GPX Viewer or another application that supports GPX. I also included a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat. It provides another way to export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app. The repository documentation explains that option. Clearing the Tracker Cache After saving your route, you can clear the device's cached positions so they no longer replay into the app. T1000E: Press the button three times. T096: Long-press to open the tracker menu, select Clear Cache, and confirm that you want to clear it. On the T096, the counter returns to 0 of 500. After I cleared the cache and reconnected, the old saved route no longer arrived. A current location could still appear, but that was a fresh position rather than the previous cached history. If you want to remove the route from both places, clear the app's history as well as the device's cache. Export anything important first. Installing the Firmware and Exploring the Code I put the firmware, source changes, and instructions in the tracker-firmware GitHub repository. It includes builds for the T096 and T1000E, device-control documentation, installation notes, and the Windows export tool. Before flashing, back up your Meshtastic configuration and export your keys. Do that first, before changing the firmware. For the demonstrated devices, installation uses the familiar flashing-mode and drag-and-drop process: Back up your existing configuration and keys. Download the firmware file that matches your device. Put the device into flashing mode. Drag and drop the matching firmware file onto the device's flashing drive. The flashing instructions shown for the T096 use two presses of Reset to make the drive appear. For the T1000E, hold the button while connecting the charging cable. Follow the repository's device-specific instructions rather than assuming that every Meshtastic board flashes the same way. How the modification fits into Meshtastic I used Meshtastic 2.8.1 for the demonstrated build. The tracker changes can also be incorporated into another firmware version and compiled, rather than being tied only to that build. The source changes are concentrated in four files. Part of the work changes the button-handling thread, because the tracker needs those additional button actions. The rest uses Meshtastic's optional add-on modules, which provide a place for custom functionality to run inside the firmware. I also compiled an ESP32-S3 version, mentioning Heltec V3 and V4 hardware as additional targets. That is separate from the hands-on T096 and T1000E examples here, so check the available files and instructions for your particular board. The LoRaWAN edition is a separate project I have a similar tracker project for the T1000E LoRaWAN edition, with comparable single-press and double-press controls. That project is aimed at LoRaWAN rather than Meshtastic. Do not confuse the LoRaWAN-edition firmware with the Meshtastic tracker build. There are supporting write-ups and architecture diagrams on the resource hub, but the firmware must match the device edition and the system you intend to use. What I like about this modification is how little it changes the everyday experience. It is still a Meshtastic node. It simply remembers where it has been, so you can take it out on its own and bring the route back afterward. Try the Offline GPS Tracker Firmware Get the T096 and T1000E firmware builds, source changes, installation instructions, and Windows GPX export tool. Get the Firmware on GitHub Frequently Asked Questions Does offline tracking stop the device from working as a Meshtastic node? No. The modification adds local location caching while retaining normal Meshtastic communication, including position broadcasts and message reception. Does the tracker save a point every minute without a GPS location? The automatic recording interval is one minute, but the device needs a GPS position available to save a location point. Why do deleted tracks return when I reconnect? Deleting position history in the app does not remove the points cached on the device. Reconnecting allows the node to replay them. Clear the device cache if you no longer want those saved positions to return. Can I export tracks without the Meshtastic phone app? Yes. The repository includes a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat that can export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app.
